newsitem.title: USA: Baseball players, owners see progress on antitrust.
newsitem.headline: Baseball players, owners see progress on antitrust.

text.p: Baseball's major league owners and players have agreed on proposals to repeal aspects of the game's 75-year-old exemption from antitrust laws, Senate Judiciary Committee chairman Orrin Hatch said Tuesday.
Hatch, a Utah Republican, said the agreement between the players and owners was "a momentous occasion."
"I think it is safe to say that the most important impediment to passage of baseball antitrust reform has been elminated," he added.

The agreement would apply to the labour law aspects of the antitrust exemption that dates back to 1922. Details of the agreement between the players and the owners were not released at the judiciary committee hearing.

But repealing the labour aspects of antitrust exemption would mean baseball owners would in effect play by the same rules as professional basketball, football and other sports follow, and players would have the same labour rights. The repeal would not apply to baseball's minor leagues.

"No other business or professional or amateur sport is blessed with the exemption from law that Major League Baseball has enjoyed and abused," said Sen. Patrick Leahy of Vermont, the senior Democrat on the Judiciary Committee.

The agreement between owners and players is narrower than an antitrust exemption bill drafted by Hatch. His version would have touched on other aspects of the baseball business. A virtually identical version of his bill died last year.
Moreover, the National Association of Professional Baseball Leagues, the minor league organisation, has not yet publicly endorsed the terms agreed by the players and owners.

Hatch said he and other members of the Judiciary panel would have to examine the alternative language to see whether it meets their central goals, or whether they would push ahead with more expansive legislation.

Hatch received a letter from acting commissioner Bud Selig, who had declined to attend the hearing or send a representative in his stead, confirming that an agreement had been reached with the players.
Donald Fehr, executive director of the Major League Players Association, did testify before the panel and said both sides had agreed.

Fehr said baseball's eight strikes and lockouts in 25 years was more than football, basketball and hockey combined. "We believe that this results, in significant part, from the belief of the major league owners that major league players ... have no rights under the antitrust laws," he said.
Both sides had agreed last November to work on this issue and lobby Congress to repeal the antitrust legislation with regard to major league labour relations. But it took months to follow through.
Among other things, the antitrust exemption now bars players from lodging unfair labour complaints with the National Labour Relations Board.

Hatch has been working on this issue since a players' strike led to the cancellation of the World Series in 1994. His bill is named for the late Curt Flood, a star outfielder with the St. Louis Cardinals in the 1960s who went to court rather than be traded to Philadelphia without his consent.
Flood lost that initial challenge but paved the way for other action to elminate baseball's reserve clause and let players move from team to team as free agents.
